the fervor set down above before Matins; and let the conscience be cleansed if anything has been committed against its purity. Nevertheless, if the mind has been raised in contemplation of divine love through continual desire, it will have less need of the exercises of little ones.

At the Second Signal.

When the second signal sounds, both for Prime and for the remaining hours of the day, let the manner set down above for Matins be observed, insofar as the time allows each one to pray. But when our cenobite enters or leaves the church, let him not neglect to show reverence to God before the altars and the crucifix, but, humbly bowing, let him say the fitting prayers according to custom. For the modest bowing of the body is held to be a sign of the inner man well ordered toward God.

In the Chapter-Room after Prime.

As the devout cenobite goes after Prime into the chapter-room, let him remember to give thanks to God for the victory of the holy martyrs, whom he knows to have served as soldiers for the Lord, in the greatest fervor of spirit, despising the torment of their own [bodies?], through the witness of death. Therefore, when you hear the brave deeds of the saints read, pray to the Lord that by their merits he may deign to forgive you your sins, and mercifully strengthen you to bear the yoke of monastic discipline, so that you may attain fellowship with them. And this desire is set before you to take up when, after their passions have been read, divine help is invoked three times by all. We do these things also at the beginning of the day, so that, strengthened to patience by the examples of the saints, we may fear no adversities throughout the whole day. But when you hear that some martyr stood bravely in the struggle of the contest, you will pray to God in these or similar words.

Prayer.

Holy soldier of the eternal King, I beseech you by the love of our Lord Jesus Christ, who made you overcome the torments of the flesh and the treacheries of this world: pray for me, that I may deserve to come as quickly as possible to fellowship with you.

If the name of a confessor, or of a virgin, or of a saint of another condition, has been recited, the devout lover of God will easily vary the prayer ex tempore to any saint according to the ardor of his affection. For affective prayers are more effective than all others.

At the Reading of the Rule.

When the reader recites, according to custom, one passage from the Rule, let the devout cenobite say in his heart: Help me, most sweet Lord Jesus Christ, that I may be able to live according to this norm of your religious servant Benedict, and to persevere faithfully at all times in your most holy service.

Then let him consider that just as the Rule is read daily for the advancement of the good and devout, so for the lukewarm, the wicked, or the negligent it is recited to the increase of damnation, so that they may be without excuse. Finally, let him know that he is bound to faithful effort in all the things that the Rule contains, just as the tenor of his profession states. For thus he said in his profession: I promise obedience and conversion of my morals according to the Rule of Saint Benedict.

When the Names of the Dead Are Recited.

But when, after the reading of the Rule, the names of the dead have been recited, the monk will pray thus for these and for all other faithful departed, entrusted and not entrusted to him, no less out of charity than out of duty.

Prayer.

I beseech you, most sweet Lord Jesus, by the pain of your wounds and by the shedding of your most holy blood, and by the power of your most innocent death: have mercy on these souls, and on all those entrusted to me in prayer, and on all the faithful departed, and grant them everlasting rest. For it is a great work of mercy to intercede before the merciful Judge for souls placed in the prison of purgatory, and to come to their aid out of charity through the remembrance of the Lord's Passion. For I firmly believe and with pious presumption trust that the prayer which is poured out for the dead from charity alone returns doubled into the bosom of the one who prays. For the devout man who here, through the fervor of divine love, by praying especially for all the faithful departed, [unclear] them in charity

On the chapter of faults

Since nothing in human actions is perfect in every respect, let the devout cenobite rejoice that he has found a remedy for his imperfection, because whatever is committed in well-reformed monasteries through human frailty is corrected daily. For the chapter of faults, continued each day, washes away public offenses; sacramental confession, repeated daily through the grace of contrition, remits hidden negligences. We discern four chapters in the monastery, of which we shall speak in order.

The first chapter is passive, when a brother proclaims himself or is proclaimed by another.

The first chapter is called passive, in which our devout cenobite proclaims himself for his negligences, or is proclaimed by another. In this chapter the lover of God, who has denied his very self to himself, humbly both accuses his negligences and suffers himself to be accused of them by others, lest he be judged more harshly by the Lord after this life. For the holy apostle of God says: If we judged ourselves, we would certainly not be judged. And the prophet Nahum says: Affliction shall not rise up a second time. For indeed, he who here, for his sins and for love of God, is now voluntarily afflicted, is worthy, as one well purged, to be freed by the mercy of the Creator from future affliction.

Would that all cloistered persons knew how greatly capitular proclamations, voluntarily endured by them, would profit toward the merit of eternal life: they would endure all accusations and injuries for love of God with inestimable joy. For we merit more when we patiently suffer injuries and adversities for love of God and brotherly charity than if we devote ourselves to good works.

Therefore, let the devout monk, standing in judgment, fear no proclamations whatever, but desire to be accused by others in memory of the Lord’s passion, knowing that before him the height of glory has been set forth, and is to be conferred in heaven upon humble patience. O brother, why would you not endure the proclamations of the brethren, you who expect the fellowship of angels? Let all indignation be far from you; let murmuring be far away; let pride withdraw far off. For you have no cause for impatience. For you are proclaimed either justly or unjustly. If justly, why would you not endure it? It is better to be purged here in small matters than after this life in many. And he who sins publicly is to be rebuked before all. But if you are proclaimed unjustly, remember that you are a monk, and you will find that you are bound to injuries. For when you are proclaimed justly, know that you are to be purged through humble patience; when unjustly, you show yourself a true monk and merit more. Therefore, when you are proclaimed, recall to memory the fourth and sixth degrees of humility; and if you are a true monk, pray even for those who accuse you. For the true lover of God loves the one who proclaims him all the more, and always on the same day bestows upon him either some prayer or some special service.

If you are good and wise, proclamation will not be able to displease you; but if you are evil and foolish, you are worthy to be proclaimed at all times. For Scripture says concerning the wise man: Rebuke the wise man, and he will love you. But concerning the evil and foolish the prophet says: They hated the one who rebuked in the gate, and they abhorred the one who spoke perfectly.

The second chapter is active, in which one proclaims another.

The second chapter we call active, in which we no longer proclaim ourselves, but another. For the act of this proclamation charity is supremely necessary; compassion also, no less than discretion, must be applied. Therefore, when you wish to proclaim your brother by reason of charity, you should always apply the fear of God; and, mindful of the fellowship of eternal life, at the beginning you should say: Our beloved brother committed this or that; I ask that he be willing to amend himself for the Lord’s sake. Whatever must be said, let him put it forward in few words and with compassion; let him state the deed simply; let him not increase the fault of the one proclaimed by aggravating it; let him silently entrust to the presiding officer the judgment whether what he did was good or bad. For he who alone among many aggravates the fault of a brother by passing sentence

Therefore he who tries to accuse another should beware lest he be moved against his brother by the zeal of bitterness; for if the charity of the accuser does not intervene, rancor does not amend the accused. The admonition of the accuser never bears fruit in the offender when the love of God and brotherly charity do not commend it. For indeed, although almighty God is supremely good, he will not give to your accusation the purpose of compunction in the heart of the brother, when he finds that you have been moved to accuse not out of charity but out of displeasure. For where he finds the root of his charity, he will not deny good fruit. But if you perceive that you have been moved against your brother by some indignation, it is better to postpone the accusation for a time than to wound yourself so cruelly with another’s wound.

The third chapter is that of private humiliation.

The third chapter of private humiliation is prescribed whenever a brother is rebuked by a senior for his negligences. For our most holy father Benedict commands, in chapter 72 of the Rule, that a monk, in whatever place or time he has been accused, as soon as he has perceived his senior’s mind to be even slightly moved, should immediately cast himself down at his feet, and there lie humbly until his command. Here he is in no way permitted to excuse himself or to place the fault on another; rather, the monk is ordered to be silent and humbly acknowledge himself. For he who is a true monk neither murmurs when justly corrected nor excuses himself when unjustly accused. Likewise in the divine offices and in the other conventual places, as soon as a devout cenobite has offended in anything through negligence, humbling himself according to the custom there, he makes satisfaction, and chooses rather to perform a greater penance in doubtful cases than to wound his conscience with a lesser one, or to cause scandal to others. But he who still understands this humiliation, to be undergone at every time and place, as burdensome and difficult, does not walk in the spirit but still lives carnally; unless, by subjugating this Jebusite, he has made it tributary to himself, he will never be a true and devout cenobite.

The fourth chapter is that of discussions and counsels.

We call the fourth chapter deliberative, when we call the brothers to counsel for some difficult matter. How this chapter ought to be held, Saint Benedict makes clear in the Rule concerning the brothers to be admitted to counsel. Therefore the humble and true cenobite, when he has been called to counsel, approaches humbly with reverence and modesty; when asked what he thinks, he speaks few words; he is by no means offended if his counsel is disregarded and another’s approved. For he states humbly what he thinks, but always preferring the counsels of others to his own; and with true subjection he commits both himself and his opinion to be examined by the one presiding. For he so annihilates himself in deep humility that he always believes more in others than in himself, and trusts that good counsel is divinely inspired in those better than himself; and in his mind he is accustomed to place his prelate before all as the vicar of Christ. Indeed, the monk especially advances toward the mortification of his own will who, in giving counsels, refers his own opinion to the abbot with cheerful humility, [unclear] from true humility, and recognizes that the occasion for pride has been taken away from him.

If after the chapter of faults one must return to the church for Terce, the manner of ordered prayer set out above is to be observed in each case. Let him also pray for his pastor; let him pray for the whole congregation, that the Lord may mercifully direct the former in his will, and, guarding the latter under regular observance, may defend it from every adversity.

Moreover let him pray for the universal Church; let him pray for the faithful and for unbelievers, so that almighty God may preserve believers in the faith and convert those who do not believe to the Catholic faith. Let him also pray for the conversion of useful persons to the order, through whom both his monastery may advance in each state and the whole observance of the order may grow for the better. Let him not forget the faithful souls in the pains of purgatory, awaiting the mercy of the Creator; but, praying for them, let him know that after a little while he will pass over to them, where the prayer now poured forth will return into the bosom of the one who prays.

But let the devout minister of Christ take care that he not neglect, on any occasion, any of the things that belong to his office, nor render the celebrant distracted by his prayers or disturbances. When there is leisure he will be able to meditate or pray in silence; when he must minister, he ought to interrupt at least vocal prayers, and, ministering diligently to the priest in all things, respond.

At the elevation of the most sacred body of Christ, he will be able, after the example of Saint Thomas Aquinas, to say attentively to Christ: “You are the King of glory, O Christ; you are the everlasting Son of the Father,” as far as the end of that hymn.

After the elevation, let the devout monk turn himself to the Lord Jesus, desiring from his inmost heart to have fellowship in so great a mystery, and let him prepare his affection as though he were going to communicate; for as often as a devout lover of God should desire from the fervor of his heart to receive the body of Christ, he is believed to have received the power of the sacrament. For the Lord Jesus said to a certain soul friendly to him: If a man fervent in my love, from desire, should wish to receive my body a thousand times in a day, if that were possible, so many times in my sight, through the power of that same body of mine, he would truly obtain his desire in his soul. And therefore, once this desire has been conceived in the mind of one who loves Jesus, let the monk pray to the Lord in this or a similar manner.

Prayer of the One Ministering.

Would that, most loving Lord Jesus, I were so well and fervently disposed that it were permitted me now to receive your most holy body in this venerable sacrament; would that it were permitted me to repeat this holy communion several times in a day. O my sweetness, O sole delight of my heart, O my hope, Lord Jesus: you know the ardor of my mind toward you, and before you is all my desire. I ask you, by all your goodness, grant me to receive the power and grace of this most holy sacrament now and at all times in my soul, so that I may be able to remain continually in you.

The Careful Preparation of the Priest Who Is to Celebrate.

[unclear] should examine most carefully. If he still finds himself a cultivator of the [first?] region, he ought not to approach the altar unless, through contrition and confession and a firm purpose of amending himself, he first strives to cleanse himself. But if he finds himself a citizen of the second region, if he has found his powers reformed and ordered toward the cenobitic end, he can readily dispose himself for celebrating, since by emptying out his own affection day by day he has learned more often to lift himself upward through desire. For divine goodness quickly enters the affection of a person who is stained by no desire of his own.

Therefore, wishing to perform this most holy priestly office with devotion and the fervor of divine love, let him first set forth some ardent prayers by which he may be able to stir himself to greater compunction. For devotion is rarely granted at the altar if the mind is not prepared beforehand for fervor. For this reason our fathers, desiring each of us to advance in his own free devotion, did not wish us to be occupied, after the manner of certain people, with many psalms before approaching the altar; not because anyone ought therefore to approach without recollection, but so that each one might be more freely able, in secret, to devote himself to exercises or prayers more suited to his devotion.

Therefore, desiring to commend to those who celebrate an elevation of the mind to the Lord Jesus before approaching the altar, we have compiled the following prayer from that which is said to be Saint Ambrose of Milan's, which we believe to be quite efficacious by virtue of the Lord's Passion. Accordingly, a devout cenobite about to approach the altar, if he has leisure and wishes, will be able to set forth this or a similar prayer beforehand, or to prepare himself in whatever ways he wishes.

Prayer before the altar

Highest priest and true pontiff, Jesus Christ, who offered yourself to God the Father as a pure, holy, and immaculate victim on the altar of the cross for us miserable sinners; who also gave us your flesh to eat and your blood to drink, and established that mystery in the power of the Holy Spirit, saying: “As often as you shall do these things, you shall do them in memory of me.” I beseech you by the pain of your wounds and by the pouring out of your most precious blood, and by the power of your most innocent death, and by your very body and blood, the price of our salvation; I beseech you by this wondrous and ineffable charity by which you so loved us miserable and unworthy ones that you washed us from our sins in blood: [unclear] all my sins, and teach me, your unworthy servant, whom among your other gifts you have also deigned to call to the priestly office, not by any merits of mine but solely by the gracious condescension of your mercy, through your Holy Spirit, to handle this mystery with that reverence and honor, devotion and fear with which it ought and is fitting.

Grant me, I beg, always to believe and understand, feel and firmly hold, say and think concerning so great a mystery that which pleases you and that which is expedient for the salvation of my soul. Let your good Spirit enter into my heart, to sound there without sound, and without the noise of words to speak within me the truth of such great mysteries. For they are very deep, and covered with sacred veils. Because of your great mercy, sweetest Lord Jesus, grant me to celebrate the solemnities of masses with a pure heart and a clean conscience. I beseech you, by the sweetness of your most holy heart, most loving Savior, free my heart from all vain, unclean, harmful, and illicit thoughts, so that it may become a dwelling-place of your love, now and without end forever.

I beseech you, O lover of humankind, sweetest Lord Jesus, by every power of your most holy Passion: drive away from me the spirit of elation and pride, vainglory and envy, lust and blasphemy, and fill my soul with the virtue of charity and innocence. King of virtues, Jesus Christ, lover of holy chastity and integrity, I beseech you by the most holy virginity of the most blessed Mother of God and undefiled Virgin Mary, and by the purity of your most reverend body: extinguish in me, with the dew of heavenly blessing, the tinder of burning lust, so that the brightness of all purity may be and remain in me. Mortify in me, I beg, the goads of the flesh, and all lustful stirrings and disordered affections, and give me true and perpetual chastity, together with the other

with your gifts, which please you in truth, so that at all times, with unstained body and clean heart, I may be able to offer to you the sacrifice of your body and blood.

I know, Lord, and truly know, and I confess this very thing to your goodness: that I am not worthy to approach so great a mystery, because of my too many sins and my many negligences. But I also know, and with my whole heart believe and with my mouth confess, that, since you are almighty, you can make me worthy, you who alone justify the ungodly, and from the unclean can make the clean.

Therefore, by your omnipotence, I pray you: grant to me, your unworthy servant, true contrition for my sins, and also pure devotion, and most fervent fear and reverence, so that with purity of heart and a fountain of sweet tears, with spiritual gladness and heavenly joy, with humility and the fervor of charity, I may be able to offer to you. O sweetest Lord Jesus, grant me in this hour your mercy, so that my mind may feel the sweetness of your most blessed presence, and the devotion of the holy angels around me, and the peaceful elevation of [itself?] in you.

Take away from me, Lord Jesus, all my iniquities, and mercifully kindle in me the fire of your love. Do not be angry with me, O Jesus, ineffable good, nor withhold the multitude of your mercies from me. For it is not in my justifications that I pour out prayers before your face, Lord, but in your many mercies. Take away from me, Lord Jesus, a stony and hard heart, and give me a heart of flesh and contrite, which may fear you, love you, cherish you above all things, delight in you alone, follow you, and enjoy you forever.

O most merciful Lord Jesus, I pray you through the most holy mystery of your body and blood, by which in your Church the saints are daily fed and given drink, washed and sanctified: give me your holy virtues, adorned with which, with a good conscience, I may be able to approach your altar, so that these heavenly sacraments may become for me salvation and life. For you said with your holy and most blessed mouth: The bread which I shall give is my flesh for the life of the world. If anyone eats of this bread, he shall live forever. O sweetest bread, heal the palate of my heart, so that I may feel the sweetness of your love.

Heal my heart, Lord, from every weakness, so that it may feel no sweetness except you, seek no love except you, love no consolation except you. O most holy Jesus, bread of life and understanding, having in yourself every delight and every sweetness of fragrance, who always refresh us from yourself and never fail in yourself: let my heart, I beseech you, eat you, and let my soul be filled with the sweetness of your savor. O holy bread, O living bread, beautiful bread, clean bread, who came down from heaven and give life to the world: come into my heart, and cleanse me from every defilement of mind and spirit. Enter into my soul; heal and sanctify me at all times. Be the protection and continual salvation of my body and soul. Repel from me the enemies who lie in wait for me, so that, fortified by the sacrament of your body and blood, I may advance through you on the straight path under regular discipline, and after this life may come gladly to your kingdom.

An Excuse for the Lengthiness.

If this prayer has seemed too long to anyone, let him read the part he wishes, since for this reason we have divided it into short paragraphs, that we might remove weariness. But the person who wants to read neither the whole nor a part complains of its length in vain, since he is shown to be unwilling to pray either at length or briefly.

Meditation Before Approaching the Altar.

For by meditation on the Lord’s Passion, or at least on one of its more sacred articles, or on several, if the opportunity of time is present, the mind of a devout person is pierced with compunction by a wondrous working, if the custom of tasteful meditation

I would indeed call meditation on the Lord’s passion savory: when a man, purified through true mortification, as soon as he has begun to turn over the Lord’s passion in thought, is dissolved into tears without violence, from love alone, and from the excessive desire of fervor is prepared as though for a certain transport of mind. He who has received this gift from the Lord will never be able to prepare himself better for celebrating than if, before approaching the altar, he always runs through in meditation, with tears, at least one article of the Lord’s passion. For indeed, since the celebration of masses was instituted by our redeemer himself in memory of the Lord’s passion, a man never prepares himself for it better and more fruitfully than if he burns more fervently through meditation on that most bitter passion itself.

The elevation of the priest’s mind to God during celebration.

With what great reverence, devotion, and purity of mind we ought to stand before almighty God at the altar, what discourse could express, or what understanding penetrate by comprehending? For there the true body and true blood of our Lord Jesus Christ are confected in an ineffable manner; there the Lord of majesty, truly present, is adored; there the army of angels, attending upon its invisible king, rejoices together; there the whole heavenly court adores Jesus, God and man. Therefore the greatest purity of mind, the greatest reverence and humility, are needed when we must stand before so great a majesty, lest the Lord Jesus, who searches the reins and the heart, be able to find in us anything that offends him. Let all worldly cares withdraw far from here; let all thoughts depart. Let nothing be thought here except what pertains to the consummation of so great a mystery; let nothing turn in the mind except what befits the presence of so great a majesty and glory. For here no office of human power is performed, but the miracle of divine majesty; the Son of God is sacrificed to the Father; the body of our redeemer is truly received; the mystery of our reparation is celebrated. Therefore the priest standing at the altar should remember that he stands before an invisible majesty, and should beware of thinking anything from any other source.

After celebration. Let careful guard be kept over the mind.

After the celebration, or after communion of the Lord’s body and blood, let the devout cenobite offer thanksgivings to almighty God; and let him keep himself throughout the whole day in the purity and devotion of mind he has begun, through spiritual exercise; let him direct his affections toward God with fiery rays, and not grow lukewarm from his holy purpose. Before all things let him strive to love nothing in this world, but to raise his heart continually to the fire of divine love, wholly stripped of all earthly affections. Let him always think how henceforth he may order his life as though anew, in the holy fervor of his way of life, and humbly dispose himself for the frequently repeated reception of so great a guest. Finally, through the day, in the labors enjoined upon him, let him often offer some prayer to God the Father in the power and union of that sacrament, so that through the exercises of holy communion and regular obedience he may inflame himself more greatly in divine love. And we attain this divine love especially through the power of this venerable sacrament, if, by receiving it more often in memory of the Lord’s passion, we are renewed through the grace of compunction. For indeed the devout mind of man, through communion of this most sacred sacrament, is kindled by the effective operation of fervent divine love; and, having wholly denied itself, is transformed into Christ through grace united [unclear]. Therefore, the more each person, denied to himself through true resignation, has offered himself as a living sacrifice in memory of the Lord’s passion, the more disposed he will be to celebrate worthily.

After private masses. Returning to the cell.

When the celebration of masses has been finished and the thanksgivings concluded according to custom, let the monk return to his cell, and after the customary prayer has been said beforehand, as above at matins:

De gloria in excelsis

Let him recollect himself for a little while, and kindle himself more fully toward the holy purpose of perseverance. Then, turning to the Lord, let him say:

Prayer.

I beseech you, most sweet Lord Jesus, through the virtue of your most holy body and blood which I have received, though unworthy: grant me the sweetness of your love, the sincerity of brotherly affection, strength in temptation, purity in heart, and discipline in conduct, so that, by your bounty, I may satisfy my profession and continually advance in your most holy love. Then, until the first signal for choir, let him read something good, meditate, or pray, or certainly write; and let him fervently apply himself to the work enjoined upon him by obedience.

At the first signal for choir before High Mass.

When the first signal has sounded for the hour which customarily precedes High Mass, the monk, immediately putting aside everything he has had in his hands, should read the preparatory prayers for choir, as they have been set out above before Matins. Afterwards let him go to choir with reverence and maturity, bowing and praying according to the rite set forth above.

At High Mass.

Consideration IV.

When the bells are rung for High Mass, you will be able to read the proper hour of the Holy Cross, and afterwards, so far as time permits, to recall to mind something from the proem set before private masses. For the sum of our salvation is placed in the merit of the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ; nor is any good work believed to be meritorious for us which is not offered in its power. The memory of this passion is enacted in the celebration of masses, where the innocent Lamb, slain for us, is offered to God the Father in an ineffable mystery. Therefore we truly hope for salvation from our Savior alone, the Lord Jesus Christ, whom we believe to have suffered for us. And so whatever the Church asks in the collects, she humbly prays that it be given to her by God the Father through him. Therefore let our devout monk keep in his heart this regard for the merit of the Lord's passion; upon it the whole office of the Mass may sweetly run, as upon a lower millstone. For every Mass, of whatever kind it may be, that is said in the holy Church of God, is at all times referred to the merit of the Lord's passion.

On the Introit of the Mass.

We do not intend, however, to explain the office of the Mass point by point, since each of our men can find many works by others; but we wish to give devout brothers occasion for meditation, whom we know to be inflamed by inward desires. Therefore you can, by meditation, refer the first part of the introit and the verse to the incarnation of the Lord, and refer the repetition with the Gloria to his nativity. Nevertheless you ought carefully to examine what the introit contains according to the literal sense, so that you may be able to find a suitable spiritual understanding for yourself. For nothing is done in vain in the divine office, but all things are filled with mysteries and sacred actions.

On Kyrie eleison.

Kyrie eleison is Greek, and is composed of a noun and a verb; and among them these are two words. For the first is from kyrios, which is “lord”; kyrie is said in the vocative. The second is from eleeo, which is “I have mercy”; eleeson, “have mercy,” is uttered in the imperative. Hence kyrie eleison is formed, that is, “Lord, have mercy,” by elision for kyrie eleison, since a vowel before a vowel can be elided for a better sound.

Therefore Kyrie eleison is said three times to the Father, so that he who, out of exceeding charity, willed that his Son be incarnate from the Virgin and die for us, may will to come to our aid in our necessities by his mercy. To the Son also we say Christe eleison three times, in which we pray to him that he may come to our aid. We also utter Kyrie eleison three times to the Holy Spirit, in which we humbly call upon him, through his ineffable goodness, to be our help.

Then “Glory to God in the highest” is said in the singular number, in which we confess the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, one sole true God in the Trinity of persons and the unity of substance. Consequently, during this angelic hymn the monk ought to be very devout and, so to speak, individually attentive to each word; in it the gift of peace is promised to men of good will, and God is humbly adored by us in various expressions.

At the Collects.

But when the collects or prayers are uttered to God by the priest, the monk, standing bowed, should think of nothing else, but, listening to the words of the priest, should present his own desire to God in agreement with them.

At the Epistle.

When the epistle is read, you ought diligently to attend to everything, and with the greatest fervor of spirit give thanks to God, because, leaving the Jewish people behind, he mercifully willed to call you and your forebears from Gentile error to his faith.

At the Gradual. Alleluia. Sequence.

At the Gradual.

Or at the tract, consider how long a desire the holy fathers had, who before Christ’s incarnation longed for his coming. Afterwards reflect with how many labors and injuries your Savior was wearied for thirty-three years in this world for your sake, he who voluntarily gave himself to death for your salvation. Then call to mind the long and perilous exile of your soul in the flesh, so that through this meditation on present misery you may be able to inflame your affection more fully toward divine love.

During the Gospel.

When the holy Gospel is read, with mind lifted up, exulting in the Lord, give thanks, because the merciful Father willed you to be born of Christian parents, and because he made you a sharer in his holy and most sweet teaching.

During the Creed.

When the symbol of the Catholic faith is sung, consider all the words and mysteries with humble fervor of spirit. Hasten at once to recollect yourself wholly within yourself, so that you may be able to give thanks to him who called you to the faith without any merit of your own, and [unclear] to raise yourself through love of the Spirit. Think, if you can, or rather as much as you can, how great, exalted, and immeasurable is the Son of God, who willed to be incarnate for you; how hard and bitter were the things he endured for you.

At the Offertory.

At the offertory apply your mind, together with the host to be consecrated, in offering; weigh what is done there mystically. For the host is round and white. In its whiteness are set forth the purity, innocence, and suffering humanity of our Savior, to be offered to God the Father on our behalf against all our impurities; in its roundness his immeasurable divinity, set before us as a reward, is offered. Therefore say to the Lord:

Prayer.

I have no worthy gift to offer you, almighty God; as a sacrifice I hand myself over to you. Therefore, holy Father, receive me, in union with the most holy offering of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, your only-begotten Son, as an eternal gift to you and as a perpetual servant; and give me the continual fire of your holy love, that I may be able always to render you service pleasing to you. Through the same.

Prayer.

I offer to you, almighty God, the life, passion, and death of the same our Lord Jesus Christ: for my sins; for the holy Roman and universal Church; for the supreme pontiff; for our bishop; for our abbot; for all my brethren; for the unity of our observance; also for our whole order; for the salvation of all the faithful; for the conversion of unbelievers; and for the redemption of the souls of the faithful who are in the pains of purgatory. I beseech you, holy Father, receive this offering of mine in union with that charity with which you received the same our Lord Jesus Christ as he died for us on the cross, and may it be pleasing to you.

During the Preface.

At the preface take care to raise your mind from all earthly things to heavenly things, and to prepare it to praise the Lord with the holy angels. Remember that through the merit of the Lord’s

of the Passion you have been called to the fellowship of the angels; and take care that you come to it through observance of the commandments.

At the Sanctus.

With your mind lifted upward when the Sanctus is sung, glorify the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, one God and Lord; humbly adore his majesty with the holy angels at all times.

During the Canon.

After the Sanctus, during the Canon, you may take up meditation on the Lord’s Passion, and offer it, through each of its greater principal articles, to God the Father, for yourself, or for others, or for any necessity. Say, therefore, in this or a similar manner:

Holy Father, I offer to you the bloody sweat and tears of our Lord Jesus Christ, your most beloved Son, in that charity and union by which he voluntarily offered himself to you unto death for us: for my sins, or for that brother, or for this or that necessity; and I beseech you, through the pain of the wounds of the same your sweetest Son, and through the pouring out of his most holy blood and the power of his most innocent death: have mercy on me, or on him, or grant us this or that, etc. Through the same our Lord.

You may also act in like manner concerning the other articles of the Lord’s Passion, and enlarge them in offering according to the intention of your affection.

At the Elevation.

If, at the elevation of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, your mind has not been occupied with higher things, you may pray to the Lord, who is truly present, in this way.

O Christ, king of glory. You are the everlasting Son of the Father. You, to deliver, etc., to the end. For Thomas Aquinas is read to have prayed this part of the hymn to the Lord at the elevation.

At the Agnus Dei.

When the Agnus Dei is sung, raise your mind to the Lord Jesus with singular trust, and humbly pray that he receive you into perpetual peace. Direct your affection toward him for love of whom you have left all things; ask from him a stable progress in your holy purpose through reception of sacred communion.

At the Ite, missa est.

When at the end the Ite, missa est is sung, see that your mind is lifted up with the holy angels returning into heaven, so that through desire you may merit to behold the Lord Jesus presiding in majesty, whom, having been sent to the Father in the sacrament, you can no longer see on earth. Therefore kindle your desire through the image of desolation, in the manner of those who are separated unwillingly from their friends.

Say, then, in your heart:

Meditation.

Behold, my Lord has returned to the heavens; he has left me desolate on earth. What am I doing here among mortals, who have an immortal Lord? Why do I not follow him? Woe is me, for my sojourning has been prolonged; I have dwelt with the inhabitants of darkness; my soul has long been a sojourner. I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ; but who will deliver me, unhappy man, from the body of this death? O most beloved Lord Jesus, O my hope, O God and savior of my soul, draw me after you; I shall run in the fragrance of your ointments. O my sweet love, do not forget me at the end, but deign frequently to lift up my mind to you, so that, since I, placed in this mortality, am unable to see you bodily, at least uplifted by affection and desire in your most holy love I may merit often to behold you in spirit in glory. O my salvation, O heart of my heart, most beloved Jesus, do not abandon me or despise me; be a gracious helper to me, and direct me always in your most holy will, so that I may truly be able to please you.

After High Mass and the Following Hour.

After the end of the hour that immediately follows high mass, return to your cell with the customary reverence described above; pour out prayers to the Lord through fervor of spirit, as we taught after Matins; what remains of the time

persist in these meditations. Consider the foulness of sin, which separates from God and condemns forever the man who has turned away and does not repent. Take care, therefore, to turn your will wholly to God with a most firm resolve, and to avoid, with all your strength and at all times, the contagion of sin.

On Regular Refection.

When the signal is sounded for refection, feel heartfelt compassion for the sick, the needy, and the poor who suffer want; and when you can do nothing else for them, beseech the Lord on their behalf. Consider that among Christians there are many far better than you whom harsh poverty oppresses in this life, to whom not even the food necessary for sustenance is offered at this hour, nor even the thinnest garments supplied to clothe the body. But you, though you are a monk and a despiser of the world, clothed in the best garments, sit at table like a prince; food is set before you to satiety by brothers better than yourself; all necessities are ministered to you, an unworthy sinner, by God’s servants, even to the point of nausea. Consider, therefore, what outcome this abundance of things will have in a monk, since you, who by entering religion professed poverty, now in religion feast more splendidly than the rich of the world. Take care, therefore, not to be ungrateful to God for such great benefits; live according to the rule which you have professed; pray for those who contribute temporal substance to your monastery, that almighty God may mercifully grant them eternal life.

On Table Reading.

When you are sitting at table, be composed while eating; do not look about here and there, but be intent on eating the food set before you only for nature’s necessity, with humility and thanksgiving. Consider diligently what is read at table, so that just as the body is refreshed by its food, so the soul may by no means be deprived of its own refection. Learn, while eating, often to raise your mind to heavenly things, and by the word of sacred reading, which is never lacking to us as we eat, sweetly to inflame yourself with divine compunction. For the cleric and inward worshipper of God, whenever he hears anything read, even at meals, about the bitterness of the Lord’s passion, about the fervor of divine love, or about the kingdom of the heavenly homeland, at once groans with excessive desire; his affection is kindled in the ardor of love; compelled by exceeding sweetness, the man sheds tears. For truly the mind that genuinely tastes God as sweet, as soon as it hears his name or looks upon the image of the crucified, is dissolved in compunction and is lifted by affection to his feet or his embrace.

At the Thanksgiving.

When refection is completed, give thanks to the Lord; and when, under the psalm, you go to the church, direct your mind upward; intercede for benefactors, living and dead. If after the thanksgiving you add some special prayer for the dead, you do well.

On Regular Reading.

Leaving the refectory for your cell, if it is not a fast day, fulfill the accustomed prayer; then read something good for edification; meditate, or do the work that has been assigned to you, or write. But if it is a fast day, take up the volume of your study and enter the place of regular reading; sitting with the others, read in silence what you wish. But if you are asked by the president to say something good, you will answer humbly with a few useful words and without curious citations. Use plain speech, and do not bring forward the vain curiosities of secular people; do not entangle the brothers sitting around you or your superiors in your discourses, but express the conception of your mind simply in few words, unless perhaps the president, for a definite reason, orders you to make a longer discourse.

The Monk’s Exercise after Dinner until Vespers. Consideration VI.

After the reading, when you have returned to your cell, you should always put some prayer before your works and seek God’s help in everything you do. But when you are in your cell, do not be idle; rather, do something good, especially what the obedience of the abbot has enjoined. Now write; read something good or meditate, because in his cell an idle monk makes either a beast or a demon. But of these things we shall speak in their proper place in what follows. Take care to spend the time usefully, because concerning all these things you are shortly to render an account to God.

On Dwelling in the Cell and the Works to Be Done in It.

There are three places in which a devout monk and lover of God ought frequently to be found: namely, in the church, in his cell, and, at the proper time, in the refectory. But he must not allow himself to wander about the monastery, because it is written of the wicked, the reprobate, and the gyrovagues: “The ungodly walk in a circuit.” But of the just man Jeremiah says: “It is good for a man when he has borne the yoke of the Lord from his youth; he shall sit solitary and be silent, because he has raised himself above himself.” The works of the cell, however, are few. The first is to attend to commands; the second is to read profitably; the third is to devote oneself at fitting times to meditation; the fourth is to pray frequently; the fifth is to rest becomingly. Let us speak briefly of these in order.

First, in the cell you must attend to commands:

First, then, while you are in the dwelling of the cell, learn to attend to commands, and not to prefer your [unclear] devotions to obedience. For Scripture says: “Obedience is better than sacrifices, and to hearken is better than to offer fat.” Therefore, if something has been assigned to you to do in the cell, do not transgress the paths of obedience on any pretext, but strive diligently to perform the work imposed on you for the love of our Lord Jesus Christ and the merit of holy obedience. Hence Hugh, lover of quiet, says: “Be gladly in the cell, and always do something in it that may edify you and has been enjoined by a superior, considering that you have no right to leave it without permission, except for the necessity of nature.” You have also on this matter the prohibition of our most holy father Benedict in the Rule, who forbids you exit and wandering without permission.

Second, in the cell one ought to read profitably.

It especially befits a monk, while he is in the cell, always to read something good and to occupy himself profitably in all things. For sacred reading overcomes the temptations of the devil, calms the fires of the flesh, makes one despise the world, and lifts the mind to heavenly things. For Jerome, lover of divine Scripture, truly said: “Love knowledge of the Scriptures, and you will not love the vices of the flesh.” Not all things are to be read by all monks, since he who is still weak in spirit must be imbued only with simple teachings. And Hugh says to the monk who loves simplicity: “Do not read in order to be considered more learned, nor read curious things that do not edify, since vain reading begets vain thoughts and extinguishes devotion of mind.” Therefore simple things, not lofty ones, are to be read by the simpler monks; devout things, not curious ones, so that those who, because of slowness of understanding, are not learned in higher matters may not become dissipated in vain ones. But for those who are stronger in spirit we do not forbid studies suited to them, since all things are clean to the clean, and nothing read harms the truly devout. Nevertheless, let no one claim for himself a strength of spirit that he does not have; rather, it is placed in the abbot’s discretion to judge who seems fit for freedom of reading.

Third, in the cell you must devote yourself at fitting times to meditations.

As a flower springs from the root, so meditation is generated from reading. If the reading has been vain, the meditation too will be fruitless and useless. For meditation is the fruit of reading, and prayer is the offspring of meditation. Take care, therefore, to devote yourself at fitting times to holy meditations, so that you may sometimes also build up the mind and lift it, through the fervor of divine love, into contemplation. Finally, meditation itself lifts the mind.

Cū pergis ad stratũ tuũ prius aliquid

and commends the zeal for reading to memory.

Fourth, you ought often to pray in the cell.

The holy apostle admonishes us to persist in prayer without interruption, because, just as breath is always necessary for us for the life of the flesh, so continuous prayer is altogether necessary for the health of the mind. For just as by readings we are instructed toward good, so by prayers we are freed from evil. For the Lord says in the holy Gospel: Pray, that you may not enter into temptation. For prayer refreshes the hungry mind, extinguishes the fire of carnal desire, instructs morals, and drives away demons. If you wish always to be with God, always pray. Let your prayer be pure, simple, and clean; let it be poured out to God through the fervor of love, and it will not be able to be unfruitful.

Fifth, you ought to rest properly in the cell.

He rests best who commits no evil. He rests well who despises all the occupations of the world. Be quiet in the cell, so that you do not wander this way and that with any thought; be pure and tranquil in mind, so that you may deserve to attain savory knowledge. For Saint Prosper says in a poem: Wisdom imbues a tranquil mind, empty of cares, and will be the guest of a peaceful breast. And again he says: Those who are quiet can scrutinize the law in some measure, if hearts free from the noise of the world are at leisure. Therefore, so that the mind intent upon pious studies may be aided, let divine love overcome carnal quarrels. Therefore remain quiet in the cell, and by loving you will be able to know the truth. For the mind will not be able to be tranquil and receptive of divine wisdom when the body is restless. Hence Hugh says: In the dormitory be quiet, lest another be disturbed through you. But waking or wishing to sleep, let the memory of God’s goodness always occur to you with thanksgiving, because he himself always watches over us, so that he may guard us, humbly serving him, from every evil. about thinking or meditating on God, you ought to set beforehand, so that amid holy thoughts you may be able sweetly to fall asleep. For such as the occupations of one awake have been, such also will be the repose of one sleeping, and such will be his dreams. For the mind, burning with divine love, will be able, neither sleeping nor waking, to forget its beloved, as the bride says in the Canticles: “I sleep, and my heart keeps watch.”

At Vespers. Seventh Consideration.

When the first signal for Vespers has been heard, and, according to custom, “Blessed be the name of the Lord” has been said, with the other things customarily set before it, have compassion on those occupied in secular business, and give thanks to almighty God that he has willed you to be free from those things for serving him. Then you will be able to gather yourself back to inward things, or to meditate somewhat on the Passion of the Lord, until, when the second signal sounds, you go to choir. For in my judgment there is no better meditation for beginners and those making progress, for compunction and devotion of mind, than that which takes its beginning from the Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ through ardent affections.

At the Vigils of the Dead.

When compelled by the vigils, after Vespers you will be able to perform the hour of the Holy Cross, and afterward to think somewhat about the immense charity of God with which he loves faithful souls. Then, as much as you can, consider in how great desolation those holy souls placed in purgatory are; how great is the pain for a spirit separated from the body and desiring to return to the center of its beginning, not to be able to behold the countenance of its Creator through friendly fruition, but to be compelled to wait in punishments and torments most grievous to it. For so great is the desolation, sadness, and grief of a soul separated, placed in punishments, and desiring to come to God, that no kind of torments known to us in this world could be compared with its sadness. There is no comparison, in our manner of speaking, of bodily sadness and desolation with the state of a separated spirit, placed in delay of return to its beginning.

At Nocturns. Seventh Consideration.

Whence the aforesaid hour of the dead seems to be held as night, which is nocturnal. For although nocturns do not end the day, but are continued through the night, for that reason it is now called nocturnal, as if he had said night; nevertheless today he says nocturnal. And this he does, as is said in the book of the holy father Benedict, who says: Nocturns are an hour between Matins and Vespers. At Nocturns. Seventh Consideration. Consideratio .viij. Ost vesperas seu vigilias mortuoꝝ ad cellam tuā cũ oracōnibus et inclinacōnibus cōsuetis reuertere: ibiqꝫ flexis genibus gratias cōserua¬ tori tuo misericordissimo redde: qm̄ te nō solū a seculi vanitatib⁹ cleme̓ter eripuit: sed etiā a multis malis et periculis in ordine custodiuit. Deinde recogita quāta bona corꝑalia et spūalia pius tibi pater nihil merenti ex¬ hibuit: et qd̓ maximū est tibi fideliter in ip̄ius amore ꝑse ueranti seip̄m in premiū ꝓmisit. Esto gratus et semꝑ in oratione vigilās: vt in amore dei dulciter ardeas. Acto autē signo ad cenā ad occur¬ rendū te humiliter p̄para: et que superius ad pran¬ dium signauimus obserua. Post cenā ad cellā tuā redire poteris et oracōni vel meditationi inistere: donec signū pulsetur ad collationē. Ad cenā audito signo collationis spūalis mox ad eam cũ grauitate studeas occurrere: et lectionē diei vltimā cũ feruore spūs audire. Uerbū enī sancte exhorta cōuis qd̓ vltimo auditū fuerit: mēti ꝑ totā noctē tenacius inherebit. Si autē ieiani fuerit: collatio inter bibendū obseruari in refectorio cōsueuit. Ad sacrā igit̉ lectionē in om̄i loco esto intētus: qm̄ vbi verbū exhortacōnis sancte cū attencōne libenter accipit̉: non potest fieri quin mens sepius eleuetur. Ad cōpletoriū. Adens ad completoriū dn̄m exora quatenus omnia mundana et carnalia te semꝑ faciat con¬ temnere: donetqꝫ tibi in suo sanctissimo amore ingiter ꝑmanere: vt cursu p̄sentis vite cōpleto templū dei nō manufactū merearis ingredi: et ineternū cũ om̄ibus sanctis in dn̄o letari. In fine autē completorij cũ pulsari

Have compassion, therefore, as much as you can, on the desolation of the faithful souls groaning in the prison of purgatory, and pour out diligent prayers for them to the Lord. For even if, by his justice, the almighty and merciful Father delays them from the kingdom, nevertheless he loves them with inestimable charity. Therefore whatever good you now do for them by praying, you offer as a pleasing sacrifice to almighty God. And when you come there, you will receive multiplied whatever you have done here for them in charity. For Scripture says: It is holy and wholesome to pray for the dead, that they may be loosed from sins.

Passing through the cemetery, or the precinct. Pray for the dead.

When, however, passing through a cemetery, a precinct, or another place of burial of the dead, do not forget your brothers and all the departed, but, moved by charity, have compassion on them, and strive to aid them before the Lord in this or a similar manner.

¶ Prayer

Hail, faithful souls; rest in holy peace. May he who redeemed you with his precious blood deign to free you from punishments and lead you to eternal joys, where you may rejoice and exult forever, blessed ones.

¶ Another

May God the Father, who created you, bless you. May Jesus Christ, who redeemed you with his most precious blood, bless you. May the Holy Spirit, who by his mercy and gift preserved you from eternal damnation, bless you. Amen.

Read the following prayer often

I beseech you, most sweet Lord Jesus, Son of the living God, by the pain of your wounds, and by the shedding of your most holy blood, and by the power of your most innocent death: have mercy on the souls of all the faithful departed who are in the punishments of purgatory, and give them a dwelling-place of eternal light with all your saints.

After vespers until compline.

Consideration VIII.

After vespers or the vigils of the dead, return to your cell with the customary prayers and inclinations, and there, on bended knees, give thanks to your most merciful preserver, because he has not only mercifully snatched you from the vanities of the world, but has also guarded you in the order from many evils and dangers. Then think over how many bodily and spiritual goods the loving Father has bestowed on you, though you deserve nothing; and, what is greatest, that to you, faithfully persevering in his love, he has promised himself as a reward. Be grateful, and always watchful in prayer, so that you may sweetly burn in the love of God.

But when the signal has been given for supper, prepare yourself humbly to go to it, and observe what we noted above concerning dinner. After supper you may return to your cell and devote yourself to prayer or meditation, until the signal is struck for the collation.

At supper, when you have heard the signal for the spiritual collation, strive at once to go to it with gravity, and to hear the final reading of the day with fervor of spirit. For the word of holy exhortation which has been heard last will cling more tenaciously to the mind throughout the whole night. But if it is on fast-days, the collation is customarily observed in the refectory while drinking. Therefore be attentive to sacred reading in every place, because where the word of holy exhortation is gladly received with attention, it cannot happen otherwise than that the mind is often lifted up.

At compline.

Going to compline, beseech the Lord that he may always make you despise all worldly and carnal things, and grant you to remain constantly in his most holy love, so that, when the course of this present life has been completed, you may be worthy to enter the temple of God not made by hands, and to rejoice forever with all the saints in the Lord. At the end of compline, however, when [unclear] is rung

when you have heard the sign of the angelic salutation, you shall humbly greet the most blessed Mother of God and Virgin Mary, that by her merits she may guard you through the night and continually intercede with her Son for your salvation.

After Compline.

When Compline has begun [unclear], return at once to your cell; and, after the customary prayers have been said, take care to prepare yourself most diligently for the following recollection of mind.

On recollection after Compline. Consideration IX.

Since we cannot remain wholly unmoved in one holy state of mind, it is necessary for us often to renew our holy purpose, so that as often as during the day, by wandering through the byways of sins, we withdraw from the one first principle of our soul, the most high God, so often by contrition and compunction we may return to him, with amendment firmly purposed.

Hence our holy fathers established for us that we should attend to recollection after Compline, and examine ourselves concerning the negligences committed during the day, so that the purpose of holiness, which we know to be quite weak and infirm, we may renew to fervor of spirit through the continual exercise of recollection. Therefore our devout monk, wishing to recollect himself fruitfully and with useful continuation, ought principally to examine himself in order in five matters.

The first thing to be observed in recollection. The rendering of account.

The rendering of account is the rendering of account by which the monk is bidden to bring back before the eyes of his mind, for chastisement, whatever he remembers himself to have committed during the day by negligence, or badly, or less well, by transgressing. Therefore, turned toward the Lord, with hands clasped, let him lie before his bed and say in this or a similar manner:

I give thanks to you, almighty and merciful God, for all your benefits, which you have deigned to show to me, an unworthy sinner and one deserving utterly nothing, from my youth up to this hour; for though I have deserved no good, I have received many and innumerable gifts of your goodness. Would that I could worthily give thanks to you, the highest and unchangeable good; would that, useful in your holy service, I could praise you with a pure heart and a clean conscience. But alas, with weakness, concupiscence, and evil habit prevailing, I, who ought to have clung with a pure heart and conscience to your most holy love, have offended you again and again with many negligences and faults; and as often as, according to the inward inspirations of your goodness, I have tried to rise to fervor of spirit, alas, so often I grieve that I have fallen again.

Behold, good Jesus, into how many faults, how many negligences, how many guilty acts have I fallen today alone; how many vain, how many useless, how many harmful thoughts have I admitted in so few hours; how many useless and harmful words have I uttered; how many negligences and offenses have I perpetrated in my actions this day.

Woe to me, wretched man, who could not pass even one very short day in your most holy service without impurity of heart and negligence; who today have committed so many faults and various imperfections. I confess to your goodness, O most gentle God, all my sins into which I have fallen from my earliest age; before your feet, O sweetest Jesus, I place all the negligences that I have committed today. I seek pardon, which I am not worthy to receive; I ask for grace, which I confess that I have so often received in vain. O most loving mediator of God and men, Jesus Christ, do not despise me, a wretched sinner, whom you willed to purchase with your own blood. I confess to you all the negligences into which today in any way I have fallen, and the faults that I have committed.

Here the monk, prostrate in mind before the Lord, should recall the more serious negligences to memory, and, humbly asking pardon, should lament his imperfection. Above all, however, let him reconsider whether he has offended anyone by word or deed; whether he has said anything against a brother; whether he has committed anything against charity and reverence; or knowingly saddened anyone badly. And generally in whatever matter he has acted against God, against himself, against the prelate, against

... he should strive to recall to the examination of this chapter whatever he knows he has transgressed against his neighbor, or against the rule or the statutes of the fathers; and concerning secret matters, in confession on the morrow; concerning public and regular transgressions, in the next chapter, by accusing himself, he should faithfully and sincerely purpose to clear himself. Let him grieve for what has been committed; let him make satisfaction for [unclear]; let him beware of things to be committed.

Then let him consider the grave danger of offending God, whether the sin be venial or mortal. For John Gerson, chancellor of Paris, says in his treatise On the Spiritual Life: “Even venial sin is so much against God that by his justice he could damn a man eternally for it. But that he does not impute it to a man unto damnation proceeds not from justice but from his infinite goodness.” And the holy bishop Anselm admonishes us that a man ought not knowingly to commit the least sin against God’s will for the whole world. For the most blessed pontiff Augustine says: “No sin is so venial that it does not become mortal when it is pleasing.”

You would say: this opinion cannot be true, because if a sin was venial, it can never become mortal; but if it becomes mortal, it was not venial. But listen and understand. I grant that venial sin, considered in itself, cannot become mortal; but one and the same sin, which can stand together with charity, becomes merely venial for one man through negligence and weakness alone, while for another, through contempt and aversion from God in the same sin, it is without doubt rightly imputed as mortal, because it is pleasing even insofar as it is sin and against God. Blessed, therefore, is he who is always fearful; but he who is hard of mind will fall into evil. He who neglects the smallest sins when he can amend them gradually falls into graver ones.

Indeed, how greatly sin displeases almighty God is shown by the vengeance that follows. For so often in the sacred volumes and in the deeds of past time we read that those sinning against the Lord were gravely punished, that we rightly fear the pit of sin. How greatly even the briefest thought of a spirit turned away displeases him is declared to us by the fall of the first angel. As soon as [unclear] showed himself disorderly by growing proud against the Lord, he was cast into hell.

How greatly idle and useless words are against the Lord is sufficiently shown to us by the very plain story in the Lives of the Holy Fathers about the infernal pigs appearing among brothers speaking useless things.

How greatly evil and pernicious words offend almighty God was made clear in the boy of five years who blasphemed, whom the devil, snatching him alive from his father’s lap, carried off to hell, as is believed.

How greatly deeds and negligences concerning one’s office displease him is clear in the sons of Eli, who were negligent and less careful about the rite of sacrifice.

How greatly evil deeds offend God, although from infinite histories, so to speak, we can understand it, there is no need to prove by a few examples.

But when our cenobite, devout in his recollections, has found himself burdened by the things mentioned above, or by any other negligences or sins, however grave, let him assume the contrition possible to him concerning the past, the purpose of amendment for firmly avoiding future things, and penitence for what has been committed. Let him therefore take up the counsel of the aforesaid chancellor, and, moved to compunction, let him say:

“Lord my God, I confess” ¶ Truth I “to your most holy goodness that thus or thus I have sinned against your will. For this I grieve vehemently, and because I have offended you, who are wholly good, I humbly do penance.

Lord my God, you know all things concerning me.” ¶ Truth III “You know that, by your granting, I have a good purpose, and I intend, with your help, to amend myself according to my powers in the future.” But sin is avoided by prayers, by calling upon God for help; by punishments, by inflicting penance on the body; by flight, by avoiding the occasion of sin. Whoever, from sincerity of heart and without falsity in mouth or mind, shall have uttered these three truths to the Lord, however much he may previously have sinned, is now secure, if he should die in such a state even without confession, in the absence of a priest; yet in such a way that in purgatory he makes satisfaction for what he did not complete by doing penance. But he who, because of an opposing will to sin in which he actually takes delight, or because of a wicked purpose by which he scorns to avoid occasions of sins, cannot truthfully say these same truths from a pure mind, is in a state of damnation; him not even the pope can absolve.

The Appointment of Future Caution.

The second thing which is prescribed for the monk to observe in his recollection is called the appointment of future caution. Let him consider what have been for him the occasions of past transgression, and he will more easily guard himself from future danger. For never is the pit of sin better stopped up than when the occasion for sin is avoided. And Saint Bernard says: For the night as it comes on, an appointment must be made, distributing one’s exercises according to the rule of the common institution. In these every debt is duly paid, if the spirit is subjected to God and the flesh to the spirit; and if anything has been omitted, neglected, or imperfect, let it not remain unrecompensed in due manner, time, and place.

The Request for Suffrages.

The third thing in the recollection of a good monk is the devout request for suffrages: since he well understands his own weakness, he asks help from those stronger than himself. Therefore, as soon as he has completed his recollection, he turns to the holy and undivided Trinity to ask for mercy; then he invokes the most blessed mother of God; afterward he implores the prayers and aid of all the saints. And here he remembers not only himself, but pours out prayers for the whole order and the Church.

The Blessing for Resting.

The fourth thing in the recollection of the monk is the blessing for resting, by which he fortifies himself with prayers and entrusts himself to the divine goodness to be guarded through the night. Therefore, at the sound of the signal for sleeping, or at the appointed time, going to the place of rest, let him fortify himself with the sign of the holy cross, and say with devotion:

The Blessing of Rest.

May the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, the merit and integrity of blessed Mary ever virgin, the sign of the holy cross, the power of the Lord’s passion, and the blessing, guardianship, and merit of all the saints, angels, and elect of God be between me and all my enemies, visible and invisible, here and forever. Amen.

Prayer.

I commend myself this night and at all times into your wounds, most loving Lord Jesus; and I beseech you, through the merit of your most holy passion, have mercy on me and guard me from all snares and illusions of the enemy, so that with a pure mind and clean body I may be able to rise at the hours appointed for me and praise you with fervor of spirit.

Discretion for Having Rest.

The fifth and last thing to be commemorated in recollection is discretion for having rest: just as the monk should never wholly omit this evening recollection, so too he should not wish to prolong it too indiscreetly to the destruction of his head. Therefore, when all things have been completed with discretion, let him raise the desire of his fervor toward God with tears, if he can; let him not confuse his mind. But as he climbs into bed, let him carry with him in memory something of the Lord’s passion, or of the love of Jesus, or certainly of the glory of the heavenly kingdom, in which, as he sleeps, he may rest sweetly. For Bernard says: When you are going to sleep, take something with you in memory or thought, in which you may fall asleep peacefully, which sometimes may also help you to dream, which may also receive you when you wake, and restore you to the state of yesterday’s intention. Thus the night will shine like day for you, and night will be your illumination in its delights, so that you may fall asleep peacefully, rest in peace, and easily wake; and when you rise, you will be ready for redemption in that from which you had not wholly departed. Nevertheless, discretion must always be applied in all these things, lest either excessive meditation, hindering sleep, destroy the brain, or immoderate sleep, taken beforehand, cause meditation to be wholly interrupted. For at this hour the monk should rather sleep than meditate, so that in time

statuto sit ad surgendū dispositꝰ: et ad diuinū officiū cū hi lariatte aī bene ordinatꝰ. Affectꝰ em̄ ꝑ meditaconē nimiū inflāmatꝰ cerebrū et sensus destruit: et somnū ab oculis de biliū tollit. Sit ergo breuis in lecto meditatione vbi capiti vel ꝑ gratiā vel ꝑ naturā non adest magna fortitudo. De labore manuū. Cōside .x. established, he should be disposed to rise, and well ordered in gladness of soul for the divine office. For an affection too greatly inflamed by meditation destroys the brain and the senses, and takes sleep from the eyes of the weak. Therefore let meditation in bed be brief where great strength is not present in the head, either by grace or by nature.

On the Labor of the Hands. Consideration 10.

Since our most holy father Benedict, in the Rule, commending as true monks those who live by the labors of their own hands, declares them blessed, it seemed fitting to us that after the end of [unclear] we should say something about this most holy exercise. Indeed, we read that this work was commended in many ways by the holy fathers, in which we know that they advanced before God and men in no small measure. For the holy Apostle says: He who does not labor, let him not eat. And what the most learned doctor Augustine thought about this manual exercise, he shows most clearly in the book On the Work of Monks. We also read that those ancient, most holy fathers dwelling in solitude sweated not lukewarmly over the work of their hands, so that they might not incur the danger of idleness, and, living from their own labors after the example of the most blessed doctor of the Gentiles, might burden no one. Would that we too, brothers, might deign to undertake this holy exercise of laboring with the same intention and goodwill as they, so that after the end of our labor we may deserve to rest with them without end in the heavenly homeland.

Four Things Are to Be Observed by Monks in Labor.

When summoned to labor, the monk should strive to show himself such in all things that he does not lose the merit of bodily labor through dissolution of mind. For we see many among monks going out to labor in no right way, whom we perceive to seek nothing other than the enticements of the flesh. Of these, some take up useless and less necessary labors so that, in the time of the regular fast, they may have an occasion for eating. For they labor in order to eat; whether it benefits or harms the monastery, they do not care. Others are accustomed to arrange various labors so that, as if by occasion, they can run about here and there without the bridle of discipline. Others procure labors useless to the community so that they may freely indulge in vain conversations and frivolities. Others love outside labors so that, as if through opportunity and without suspicion, they may be able to see and speak with people, not to say those whom they know, secular persons and friends, for the flesh and not for God. Others, because of instability of mind, being unable to be quiet in the monastery, always seem to pant after labors. The intention of all who labor in this way is not sincere, and therefore they do not attain the excellent reward of labor. But you, brother, when you are called to labor, take care to submit your intention to the regular institution, so that you love nothing other than the honor of God, the merit of obedience, and the usefulness of the monastery; intend nothing except the advancement of the soul. And while you are at labor, do not imprudently extinguish the fervor of the spirit; do not omit the exercise of spiritual conversation, but take care diligently to observe everywhere the following four things. In outward conduct be faithful, serviceable, and benevolent; inwardly, humble and devout; in speech, sparing and edifying; in manners, composed and mature. If you keep these four things in labor, you will always return to your cell better.

Outwardly the Monk Becomes Faithful, Benevolent, and Serviceable.

The first thing that must be diligently observed by a cenobite in labor is that in laboring he should always show himself faithful to his monastery; in serving and ministering, or even in carrying heavier burdens, he should from charity anticipate the brothers; and in all words and deeds he should show himself benevolent and tractable. And Saint Bernard, lover of God, says: A serious and prudent soul prepares itself for every labor, and yet is not dissolved in it, but through it rather stretches and strives more, for it always has before its eyes not so much what it is doing as that by doing it [unclear]. The more truly it strives, the more fervently and faithfully it works with its hands, subjecting to itself the service of its whole body, in
