by which the will makes use; use, by exercise, supplies strength. The devout and faithful cenobite, who loves God in truth, does not spare himself in labor, but is accustomed to apply himself with such great fervor, cheerfulness, and fidelity to the works of his hands laid upon him, as though by his labor alone he were compelled to feed all those established in the monastery. For the most prudent soul knows that he spends himself wholly for God, whatever bodily necessity of his servants may happen to make him labor. For just as spiritual things cannot long subsist in religion without the cooperation of temporal things, so I do not hesitate to call the one who, for God's sake, supplies the bodily necessities to those serving God a servant of God. And therefore whatever a good cenobite can acquire for the monastery by his labors with right intention, he should know that he offers all that to the Lord. Nevertheless the monk should always understand that he must labor in such a way that he in no wise omits the monastic prayers, masses, and the other services of holy mother Church.

But manual work that is elaborate and undertaken out of self-complacency is deprived of the merit of obedience before the eternal Judge; and, as idle and presumed without the superior's permission, it is held liable to account. But the good cenobite, who desires to please God alone, in every creeping-in of an idle word, deed, or thought, should say to himself that saying of Bernard: If you were now about to die, would you do this thing which you are now doing, thinking, or saying? But if, were you now about to die, you would not do what you are now doing, you are very foolish, since you so boldly permit yourself, at the time of death, while you are soon to die, unto death. But if you desire to die well when it becomes necessary, do at no time what you would not do if death were already present. For whatever you have done now, after death you will find it, whether it is good or evil.

Within, let the monk be humble and devout.

Second, at the time of labor the monk ought to be devout and humble within. If he abandons the progress of inward fervor, what he outwardly acquires through labor profits nothing. Therefore, so that the soul may truly make progress while laboring, let him always recall to memory the degrees of good will written in the first [rule?]. Let him set in order meditations on the Lord's passion with the fervor of devotion, in which he may conform his labors, according to his ability, to the labors of Christ. Let him always be humble in heart through self-denial. Let him be devout in affection through the fervor of holy compunction, so that the outward labor of the hand may profit toward the [unclear] and the usefulness of the community, and the mind may not withdraw from the inward sweetness of divine love. If labor wearies the working cenobite, if heat burns him, if untimely thirst oppresses him, let the Lord's labor, which he endured for us, be recalled, and he will bear all things lightly. Therefore let him say this prayer to the Lord.

Prayer of one laboring.

Most sweet and most lovable Lord Jesus, king of heaven and earth, who for my redemption were born of the most pure Virgin Mary, and for thirty-three years were among men as God and man; and who had great labors in walking, teaching, and [unclear]; and endured thirst, hunger, heat, and cold willingly and patiently, for all of which I give thanks to you: receive, I beseech you, these very small labors of mine, though useless, which I offer in humility to your most holy [testament?], in memory and honor of all your labor and of your most holy passion; and may they please you in the union by which your most holy labors pleased God the Father. Amen.

Let our cenobite, moreover, during the time of labor, turn over in his mind the principal articles of the Lord's passion, first by recalling them as though with Christ present in the passion; then by giving thanks at his knees; thirdly by asking mercy in himself according to the likeness [of them].

Let him bring back to memory the conversations of any holy fathers or the sufferings of martyrs, and consider how great a reward and glory they now receive for their labors in the fatherland.

In speech let the monk be sparing and edifying.

Third, what must be observed by a monk in labor

[unclear]: that he speak few words and edifying ones. Scripture says: “In much speaking sin will not be lacking.” Let no monk speak without permission, if he truly desires to be good. But once permission to speak has been granted, let him speak only a few useful things, knowing that idle and jesting words are condemned by the Rule in every place. Let him establish for himself such a manner of speaking in every place and at every time, through circumspection, that by speaking he offend no one. Let him hear more willingly than he is pleased to speak, and let him not say everything that his mind has suggested, [unclear]. For thus Hugh says to the monk: “Do not pour out everything you know, like a vessel without a lid, which, as soon as it is tilted, pours out whatever it contains within itself, and lies open to all dust and uncleanness. Take diligent care that you not seem, directly or indirectly, to seek your own glory, nor reveal imprudently to anyone, from a spirit of boasting or otherwise, whatever commendable thing lies hidden in you. If you are silent about yourself and keep yourself hidden, you will be more pleasing; if you disclose and commend yourself, you will become cheap in the sight of all and will be laughed at. Beware of idle words: when we do not pay attention to such things, we slip little by little into harmful ones; from them are produced either disturbances or dissipations, or serious erosions of knowledge. Be such in your inner way of life that, through love of spiritual meditation, silence always delights you more than talkativeness.”

The cenobite should be composed and mature in his manners.

The monk should take care to order his manners both in labor and outside it, in every place, and in all things, both deeds and words, show himself mature before men. Let him be clean and humble in heart; let him be kind and useful in speech; let him be modest and grave in his gait; let him be mature and exemplary in his whole way of life. The whole man is ordered outwardly according to the norm of discipline if the effort to make progress is held the more firmly in the soul in all things. For indeed, while the monk desires daily to advance to better things, he avoids all dissipation and disorderly conduct. For a firm effort to make progress has this as its own property: that it makes the soul of the one striving very circumspect in all things. But he who does not have a firm effort to make progress for the better cannot truly be called composed, although he may seem to men to be mature. For feigned maturity quickly dissolves into open dissipation of mind where the root of discipline, the fear of God, is not present. Therefore, so that our cenobite may always be composed within and without, let him strive truly to be rooted in the fear of the Lord. For he who fears God neglects nothing. And the love of God is not idle.

What the monk’s conduct toward other men ought to be. Consideration XI.

Since we have begun to speak about the maturity and composure that must be observed by the monk before men, it seems useful to us now to say briefly how he ought to present himself to each one. For he is instructed to present himself in one way to his prelate, and in another way he is commanded to show himself to his confreres and to secular persons. To his ruler, in the place of Christ, he ought to show reverence; to his confrere, charity; to those who injure him, meekness; to secular persons, modest piety. Therefore let the monk render to each one what is his, and he will be truly composed before God and men. What he owes to God, and what to himself, has been sufficiently said above; now let us pursue the matters proposed to us.

His conduct toward the prelate, in the place of Christ, should be reverential.

First, the conduct of the monk ought to be reverential toward the prelate, as the Lord says in the holy Gospel: “He who hears you hears me, and he who despises you despises me.” For the monk who withholds the obedience and reverence due to his abbot does injury to almighty God. For, as our most holy father says in the Rule, the abbot is proved to hold the place of Christ in the monastery. Whoso

Nā si abbas tuus te monachū suū timere cōpellitur: equitatis ordo violat̉: et vbi esse suꝑ magistrū discipulus nitit̉: in euangeliū peccat̉ Claue ligit̉ ne p̄latis reuerentia et honorē subtrahas: caue ne illos ꝯtristādo dn̄m offendas: sed cura eis qualescūqꝫ sint reuerenter occurrere: et eoꝝ mandatis scd̓m euange¬liū ct regulā in om̄ibus obedire. Ad hoc regule capl̓m de bono zelo monachoꝝ sepiꝰ ad memoriam debes reducere: vt faciliꝰ ad fraternā charitatē temetip̄m

Whoever, therefore, despises the vicar of any king has undoubtedly shown contempt for the king himself. But tell me, good brother, why do you withhold due reverence from your prelate, whom you hear to be the vicar of Christ? Perhaps you consider him wicked and wholly unworthy of such an office, and for that reason you think it lawful for you to despise him? Not so, brother, not so; but consider whose place it is in which the vicar of Christ presides, and know that you honor the one who sends, not the one sent. If you wish to be Christ’s disciple, consider always for what purpose you have come, and you will never deny reverence to an unworthy prelate. For what purpose have you come? Certainly that, according to the Gospel and the Rule, you may deny yourself for God’s sake; that under another’s command you may serve Christ as a soldier; that for these things you may patiently await the eternal reward. Therefore, brother, do not, do not lose the crown of eternal happiness prepared for you in heaven because of displeasure with one man, a crown which you ought not to exchange for the whole world. Remember that you have nothing unless from your own [unclear]; you must humbly obey him as vicar of him to whom you have subjected yourself, and you must not examine either his life or his command, since it is not lawful for you to judge your shepherd. For in your profession you swore that you ought not to carry out your own will, but that you wished to obey the abbot in all things according to the Rule. The abbot, therefore, is lord of your will, not by his own assumption, but by the ordinance of God, whose vicar he also is. But the handling of another’s property against its lord’s will is theft, and you know that thieves will have no share in the kingdom of Christ and of God. Thus a monk who has made profession according to the Rule to God and to his abbot no longer thereafter has lordship over his own will; and if afterward he usurps that same will of his for himself, he commits theft and sacrilege. Nor will permission obtained save the presumptuous man, if it was obtained by threats and insults. Your abbot, O brother, is the vicar of God; to him you must render the obedience promised, not as to a man but as to God, and show humble reverence in God’s place. For whatever is rendered by subjects to their ruler is undoubtedly referred to God, whose vicar he is. Since, therefore, you have subjected yourself to your prelate for God alone and for no other cause, you should strive at all times to show yourself such toward him that he may freely be able to command you to do or omit whatever seems expedient to him, and may have no fear at all of any insolences or disturbances of your mind. For if your abbot is compelled to fear you, his monk, the order of equity is violated; and where the disciple strives to be above the master, sin is committed against the Gospel. Beware, therefore, lest you withhold reverence and honor from prelates; beware lest by saddening them you offend the Lord. Rather take care to meet them reverently, whatever kind of men they may be, and to obey their commands in all things according to the Gospel and the Rule. Believe me, brother, that the fault which is committed by a subject against a prelate is punished very severely, either in the present life or in the life to come. For it is written: Do not touch my anointed ones. Whatever your prelate commands you, you ought to receive it with such confidence that you believe God has inspired it in him.

Let the monk’s conduct toward the brothers be most charitable.

Secondly, the monk’s conduct toward his fellow brothers is commanded to have charity, through which alone peace and concord are maintained in the monastery. Let our faithful cenobite always think on, and turn over in his heart, the common joy of souls in eternal happiness; and let him continually direct the eye of his mind toward the equal condition of souls, so that his thought may not withdraw from love of future fellowship. If a brother offends you in any way by word or deed, if he has been troublesome or hostile to you in anything, do not weigh the movement of disordered sensuality arising from it; do not consider his present weakness, but lift up the eyes of your mind to the nobility of his soul, and consider what sort of fellowship in eternal happiness it will have with you. For this purpose you ought rather often to recall to memory the chapter of the Rule on the good zeal of monks, so that more easily toward brotherly charity you may [unclear] yourself

Clemēs sis. da sapienter. Ora ponendo te. martyriū cupiendo. Humilitas enī si mentē cenobite possederit: iniurias amare facit. Gradus vero humilitatis his verbis cōtinentur. may be able to stir up. Before all things beware lest you admit displeasure against your brother; for he who is often angry with his neighbor plainly proves that he does not love God. For whoever loves God with his whole heart does not admit displeasure against his faithful brother. But a monk ought to be established in so great an elevation of mind that, whatever a brother has committed against him, by considering the nature of that man’s soul he cannot be moved.

Let the monk’s conduct toward those who wrong him be gentle. Third, the monk’s conduct toward those who wrong him ought to be gentle; and this is done well only if regard is always had for their common future happiness and fellowship. To attain this gentleness of spirit, let our cenobite learn rather often to recall to mind the ways of life of the holy fathers, and faithfully consider with how much joy they received injuries. Let him strive above all, as far as possible, to imitate our Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, who not only endured the injuries and insults of the impious with a most gentle heart, but also entreated the Father for his persecutors, that they might not perish. The holy fathers, imitating this example of the Savior, were accustomed to receive injuries patiently and gently for love of God, and, what is more, to love the very persons who wronged them. To these things let the cenobite recall to mind the degrees of gentleness, which are contained briefly in these verses: Fit. Comfort. Gentle, bear contrary things. Preserve. Restrain. Rest wholly within yourself. Correct prudently. Be merciful. Give wisely. Pray, putting yourself forward, desiring martyrdom. For if humility has possessed the mind of the cenobite, it makes him love injuries. The degrees of humility are contained in these words.

The twelve degrees of humility. The first of the degrees of the righteous fears the Almighty. The second puts reins upon the allurements of the flesh. The third submits himself reverently to the abbot.

The fourth, when insults are disregarded, patiently obeys. The fifth discloses to the abbot the hidden things of the heart. The sixth stands as vile and unworthy in his own judgment. The seventh believes that he is lower than all. The eighth does nothing that the rule of the cell does not allow. The ninth does not speak while another does not ask. The tenth banishes laughter and condemns loud guffawing. The eleventh speaks a few words of reason. The twelfth always looks at the ground with head bent.

On the same matters, otherwise. Behold God, and do not do your own will; let another rule you. Endure hardships; hide nothing in your heart, but seek also the lowest things. Be refuse itself; do not wander idly; obstruct the tongue. Let laughter be sparing, speech grave, gestures humble.

Note: Peripsema ought to be read and written, not peripsima, as the ignorant read in the Epistle to the Romans; and it means filings and the cleansing of all things.

Let the monk’s conduct toward lay people be modest. Fourth, the monk’s conduct toward lay people ought to be modest, so that neither familiarity with them is excessive nor withdrawal indiscreet. Hence Hugh says: Concerning people, as far as lies in you, beware of everything that can be no good example to them, just as it befits a faithful servant of God to promote the honor of his Lord in all things and to guard against dishonor to him. Nor should you be familiar with any woman, even a holy one. For if they are discreet, by this you will please them more; but if they have been troublesome, they are the more to be avoided. Do not be suspicious. Be ready to serve the sick in humble services; be very truthful in words; let your words be as an oath, and you will edify others. Love poverty. Be chaste in all things, and everywhere God-fearing.

In all virtues and good morals to be founded, set before yourself that most renowned and most perfect example of all brightness: the life and conduct of our Lord Jesus Christ, who to

this one was sent from heaven, that he might go before us in the way of virtues, and instruct us by his example, as himself. Therefore the more the monk has taken care to conform himself to him in the way of virtues by imitation, the more like and nearer to him he will undoubtedly be in the glory of eternal blessedness. Whatever you do, always look to him, and consider how he bore himself in all things according to the Gospel and your own judgment. For since he is the best, he bore himself best in all things. Say therefore to yourself: If my Lord Jesus were present, what do you think he would do about this, or what would he now say? Certainly he would both act and speak in the best way, whom I must imitate in all things according to my strength.

General conclusion of all spiritual exercises. Consideration twelve.

Wishing at last to put an end to this work, we say that the fulfillment of all spiritual exercises consists in two things. First, in the knowledge and sense of one’s own imperfection, so that the monk may always be conscious of his weakness and remain rooted in humility. Second, in the desire and effort to come to a higher way of life, so that he may always desire to advance in spirit toward better things, and by no means withdraw from this effort. Toward this effort of advancing every cenobite ought to stretch out his mind at every moment; if he has at any time abandoned it, he incurs the transgression of his vow and the gravest danger to his soul. But let the monk beware lest the consideration of his own weakness cast aside the effort of advancing; let him beware lest that very effort despise the consideration of imperfection; but let these two so adhere to each other mutually that they never depart from one another. But if excessive consideration of one’s own imperfection has tempted the mind toward [unclear] despair of God, let him recall to memory what the holy abbot Bernard said: Let us breathe again, brothers, for even if we are nothing in our own hearts, perhaps something in us may lie hidden in the heart of God. These two considerations, of our weakness and of the divine estimation, stir up great devotion in us; thus the psalmist said: I am poor and sorrowful. Behold the first. Your salvation, O God, has taken me up. Behold the second.

Finally, it is necessary for one who wishes to occupy himself profitably in these spiritual exercises to have a joyful and free heart, and one alien to every anxiety or care of the world. For the Holy Spirit is the spirit of freedom and joy; he loves a heart free and joyful in God, and, so to speak, applauds his like. For just as a bird bound to the earth cannot lift itself up to heaven by flying, so a mind occupied with perishable things cannot raise itself to heavenly things. Nor should one wear out the spirit by excessive frequency of [unclear]; otherwise the brain is confounded, and one labors in vain through dry habit. Let the cenobite, therefore, fervent in spirit, learn always to persist in these things with moderation, and constantly to refer the cause of every exercise by intention to God, who is the beginning and end of all goodness. Let him faithfully direct his effort to fear and love of him, and fix his mind in profound humility, since he is not easily abandoned by God who is rooted in love.

Here ends the spiritual exercise of cloistered persons, by Petrus Fridbergensis, in the noble city of Mainz, on the eighth Ides of August, in the year of salvation 1498.

Here begins the compendium of spiritual exercise. Johannes Trithemius.

If the formula of spiritual exercise, published by us for the edification of cloistered persons, could seem very brief to all the devout who have leisure, nevertheless we fear that to those occupied with household business it may seem rather prolix. For while their thought is stretched out with continual solicitude in arranging the necessities of their subjects, the mind is easily wearied even by very brief spiritual exercises. Therefore, lest our monks who are either given over to exterior matters, or less devout in spiritual conversation, might be able, on the occasion of prolixity, to flee to the argument of their customary excuse, we have been ordered to abridge the same instruction, so that the fervent may keep the greater one in their devotion, and the lukewarm may not omit the lesser.

There follows the practice of spiritual exercise.

Before all and each of the Hours in general, let the devout cenobite strive to direct his effort to this end: that in his heart, by the root of His benefits, he may desire with all his strength to magnify God. Let there be in him so great a most fervent ardor of devotion, so great a compunction, and finally so great an overflowing of tears, that whoever sees him chanting psalms may be moved by his example to magnify the Lord. Secondly, let him remember that he can be stirred to charity toward his neighbor, because love is directed toward God in vain if the neighbor is hated. Therefore, when all the thorns of displeasure have been driven out, let the most devout cenobite, turned toward the Lord, pray.

¶ Prayer

Almighty, everlasting God, who, instructing us for the exercise of Your love by the manifold creation of things, commanded us to love You above all things with all our strength, and our neighbor as ourselves for Your sake: graciously grant me the grace of Your most holy love and of love of neighbor, so that, all motions of displeasure, aversion, and anger being repressed, I may always love You above all things with a pure heart, and may in no way depart from sincere love of my neighbor; so that, just as a member adhering to a wounded member suffers with it, so my mind, sincerely loving my neighbor, may deserve to be a member of our true head, Jesus Christ. Who lives and reigns with You.

¶ Another Prayer.

I beseech You, holy Father, almighty and eternal God, through the virtue of the most holy passion of Your only-begotten Son, our Lord Jesus Christ: enlighten the eyes of my heart, so that, pierced in spirit, I may see how often I have offended against Your commandments; and, cleansed by Your mercy from every stain of sin, may never offend You hereafter.

After Matins.

When Matins have been finished, while still remaining in the church, or even when placed in your cell, take up for yourself the disposition of true resignation, praying thus.

Prayer

O Lord Jesus Christ, Son of the living God, who at the morning hour, placed in the greatest anguish of Your most holy heart, after threefold prayer most fully resigned Yourself into the will of God Your Father: grant me, in the virtue of that charity of Yours, perfectly to contemn my own will in all things for love of You, and truly to resign myself at all times into the disposition of Your will and of those whom You have set over me. Who lives and reigns.

After Prime.

After Prime, when, leaving the choir, you enter the chapter-room, in memory of your most innocent Savior accused before Pilate, you will form your disposition toward humble confession, praying thus to the Lord.

¶ Prayer.

Rogo teꝑ innocentissime mor- tis tue virtutē. miserere mei sicut tu scis: cōfige timore tuo carnes meas: et oēs inordinatos motus in me cōprime: vt feruore sanctissimi amoris tui inflamatus. tepuro cor de diligā: ore laudabilē cōfitear: oꝑe pro viribus humili cōuersatione sequar. Hora prima post prandiū. Ora prima post prandiū. nisi fueris exercicijs sublimioribus occupatus: pro cognitione ꝓprie fragilitatis impetranda: tali vel simili modo ad dn̄m orabis. Oratio

Most loving and sweetest Lord Jesus, who at the first hour, falsely accused, truly confessed yourself to be the Son of God: have mercy on me and grant me, through your innocence, the virtue of true confession, so that I may humbly endure any words of those who accuse me, and may not be driven away by any reproaches from the inward tranquility of my mind. You who live and reign with God the Father.

After terce.

After terce you will call to mind how many reproaches, how many mockeries and derisions the most innocent Lord Jesus endured for your redemption; in memory of this, take upon yourself the desire for the sixth degree of humility, praying thus.

Prayer.

Sweetest Lord Jesus, who for us were pitiably scourged, mocked, derided, crowned with thorns, and spat upon at the third hour: grant me, by the power of all your sufferings, through the shedding of your most holy blood, always to be content, for love of you, with every abasement and extremity; so that, in consideration of my sins, I may humbly regard myself even as your unworthy workman, and yet may in no way grow lukewarm in your holy service.

After sext.

After sext, consider the Lord Jesus bearing his cross before all and then hanging pitiably upon it, together with the other particulars of his punishments; and, inflamed with desire for the seventh degree of humility, pray to him with fervor of spirit. Prayer.

Sweetest Lord Jesus, who for us wretched sinners, after the countless pains of your passion, carried your cross to the place of your death while your most sorrowful mother looked on; on which, cruelly fastened, you were given gall and vinegar to drink and were mocked in many ways: I beseech you, through the pain of your wounds, grant me pardon for all my sins, the grace of holy compunction, a fountain of tears, the virtue of deep humility, and continual remembrance of your most bitter passion, so that all that I am and am capable of may always serve you, and my mind may continually burn with your love.

After none.

After none, be mindful of sweetest Jesus dying on the cross; and, falling down in spirit at his knees, with tears, giving thanks with as much devotion as you can, you will pray.

Prayer.

I adore you, sweetest Lord Jesus Christ, King of heaven and earth, dying for wretched me on the cross, and I humbly give you thanks for your holy passion and most innocent death. O what shall I render to you, most loving Savior, for all that you have rendered to me? Behold, I offer myself to you; I continually desire to dwell in your most holy wounds. I beseech you, through the power of your most innocent death, have mercy on me as you know how; pierce my flesh with fear of you, and restrain in me all disordered motions, so that, inflamed with the fervor of your most holy love, I may love you with a pure heart, confess you as praiseworthy with my mouth, and follow you in deed, according to my strength, in humble conduct. I beseech you, most merciful Lord Jesus, through that most holy anguish of your heart which you endured on the cross when your most holy soul departed from your body: have mercy on my soul at its departure.

The first hour after the meal.

At the first hour after the meal, unless you have been occupied with higher exercises, you will pray to the Lord in such or a similar manner, to obtain knowledge of your own frailty.

Prayer.

Lord God, who by your great kindness created me in the first parent from the clay of the earth, so that, mindful of my humble condition, I might glorify you, my creator, in true humility: grant me, I beseech you, truly to know my frailty at all times, so that, while I consider how vile and almost nothing I am by my own merit, I may deserve to please you by your gift. Through Christ.

The Second Hour.

At the second hour after noon, let our devout cenobite summarily recall to memory the gravity of his sins, by which he has sinned against the rule, especially while living in holy religion; and, turned to the Lord, let him pray thus.

Prayer.

Almighty everlasting God, who have deigned, by the incarnation and death of your only-begotten Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, to give life, from your mercy alone, to us wretched people dead in sins: grant me, through the power of his most innocent passion, pardon for all my sins, so that henceforth I may deserve to serve you with a pure conscience. Through the same our Lord.

The Third Hour.

At the third hour after the meal, let the faithful cenobite remember his vows which he promised to the Lord, and especially the renunciation of all ownership, namely in things, judgments, and will; and, moved to compunction before the Lord in fervor of spirit, he shall pray thus.

Prayer.

Almighty and merciful God, who with kindly favor sanctify and receive the vows of your servants offered to you from faithful devotion: grant me to render all that I have promised, through the power of humility, chastity, obedience, and poverty, with such purity of mind that I may deserve, by your mercy, to come to your kingdom promised to the poor in spirit. Through our Lord.

After Vespers.

After Vespers, let our good cenobite consider how vain all visible things are; and, with his mind raised to the love of invisible goods, let him cry to the Lord with as much devotion as he can.

Prayer.

Almighty everlasting God, who wished to lead us through the visible things which you created to the knowledge and love of invisible things: grant me so to know the vanity of present things that I may always deserve to think with a pure mind upon the eternity of things to come. Another.

O God, protector of those who hope in you, without whom nothing is strong, nothing holy: multiply your mercy upon us, so that with you as ruler, you as guide, we may so pass through temporal goods that we do not lose eternal ones.

Another Prayer.

O God, who have prepared invisible goods for those who love you: pour into our hearts the affection of your love, so that, loving you in all things and above all things, we may obtain your promises, which surpass every desire. Through our Lord.

After Supper and Collation.

After supper or collation, let the faithful cenobite clothe his desire with what fervor of charity he can, for good zeal and especially for souls; and, praying to the Lord, let him say.

Prayer.

Lord God, greatest lover of faithful souls, who for the salvation of human beings willed your Son to die on the gibbet of the cross: grant me, by the example of the same your Son, to be strengthened in good zeal, and to fear no labors, no adversities, for the salvation of souls, so that, strengthened by the fire of your love, I may dare at the proper time to resist those who contradict you, and manfully set myself as a wall for your house. Through the same our Lord.

After Compline.

After Compline, with his strength gathered, let the devout cenobite enter alone into the secrecy of his heart; and let him leave outside all cares and anxieties of the world, so that, free and released from all things, he may deserve to speak with the Lord Jesus through the desire of compunction, and to be sweetly united with him through the fire of love. Therefore, when the faults of the day have been recalled summarily to the memory of examination, let him pray thus to the Lord.

Prayer.

Most merciful Lord Jesus Christ, who for our redemption willed to undergo a most shameful death: grant me, I beseech you, through the pain of your wounds, through the shedding of your most holy blood, and through the power of your most innocent death, pardon for all my sins, so that, with my conscience cleansed, I may henceforth cling continually to you through the desire of love, make daily progress in holy religion, and humbly submit myself in all things to your most holy will.

To the Son.

My body and my soul I commend to you, Lord Jesus Christ, this night and at all times, in the power and union of that love by which, hanging on the cross, you commended your beloved mother, the Virgin Mary, to the disciple; in which love, I beseech you, guard me from all snares of the ancient serpent; suppress the illicit movements of the flesh; drive far away foul and evil dreams; and repel the phantoms of the nights, so that I may sleep secure in your peace, and rise cheerfully at the hours appointed for me to your praises. Amen.

To the Father.

O Lord, holy Father, almighty eternal God, who have called us to your grace in the passion of your only-begotten Son

you have received graciously: receive, I beseech you, mercifully all the good works that, by your gift, I have performed on this day, in words, deeds, or thoughts, in the virtue and union of that charity and love by which you received the same Son, hanging and dying on the cross for us. To you, holy Father, in the faith and union of that charity, I commend myself this night and at all times, by which your Son, our Lord, when about to die, commended his spirit to you on the cross.

To Saint Mary.

Holy and immaculate Mother of God, Virgin Mary: I ask you, through the bitter passion and death of your most sweet Son, do not reject me, a wretched sinner, on account of my unclean conscience, but remember that you are the mother of mercy, and pray for me to God, whom you bore, that he may mercifully forgive me my sins, make me a fervent lover of himself, guard me this night from all snares and evils, and after the death of the flesh lead my soul to eternal life. To your protection, most blessed Virgin Mary, I commit myself this night and at all times, in the virtue and union of that commending by which your beloved Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, when now about to die on the cross, commended you to John, his disciple.

On the remembrance of the Lord’s Passion.

Since the Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ is the gate of our salvation, through which the kingdom of heaven is opened to us, we ought, with whatever devotion we can, to exercise ourselves in it very often, because we shall readily obtain the effect of our prayers if, through the love of compassion, in the virtue of his wounds, we adore the Lord. Therefore, faithful cenobite, with all the diligence I can I admonish, exhort, and ask you that, mindful of God’s benefits, you utterly neglect no day on which you do not give thanks to your Savior for the bitterness of his Passion and death. And if for any reason you cannot manage this at greater length, do not refuse to show yourself grateful to your Redeemer with at least one word. If the Lord Jesus himself revealed to those lovers of his to whom he wished that nothing is more pleasing to him, and nothing more useful to us, than to recall with thanksgiving the memory of his Passion and death, and to admonish others to do the same. Receive, then, an abbreviated word, lest a longer prayer make you weary.

With knees bent to the ground and hands clasped together, say:

I give thanks to you, most sweet Lord Jesus, for all the wounds, pains, and injuries of your most innocent Passion and death; I ask you, through that death of yours, have mercy on me now and at the hour of my death.

Or thus:

To your most bitter Passion and most innocent death, Lord Jesus Christ, with a compassionate soul I give thanks; I ask you, have mercy on me.

Or thus:

I praise, bless, and adore you, Lord Jesus Christ, King of heaven and earth, and I give thanks to you for your holy Passion, by which you delivered wretched me from everlasting death. I ask you, through the virtue of that Passion of yours, make me forever a partaker of your most innocent death.

Conclusion of this compendium, by Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim.

Lest I be more prolix than is fitting, here I put an end to the compendium. For that venerable assembly of abbots of our annual chapter instructed me to avoid prolixity in this place, lest lukewarm and worldly cloisterers call weariness as a cause. If the Lord Jesus gives me a life free from cares, as I have always desired, I shall endeavor to satisfy both my own intention and another’s request. For, when certain virgins dedicated to Christ were asking, I resolved to hand down a rule by which any devout cenobite may be able to exercise himself in the Lord’s Passion against all temptations; if he has continued, as he ought, in exercising himself in it for a few months, little by little he will sweetly fly from the humanity of Christ to his divinity by the ray of love. For to those desiring to come to the love of God, continued meditation on the Lord’s Passion opens an easy approach, because while the mind, through compassion, is pierced from the memory of the benefits of so great a lover, burning with tears and desire it is lifted up to love. Therefore you cloisterers dedicated to God, for whom there is no leisure to attend to many things, receive these few things; in them, although there may not be a continuous fire of love, it can nevertheless be renewed for those who persevere.

Here ends the compendium of daily spiritual exercise, by Johannes Trithemius, abbot.
